narrative.text: The cover page of the Arabic edition of the second edition of WHO's classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health; the extracted text is largely garbled OCR.
A page from the Arabic classification naming categories such as health system challenges and digital interventions for health managers and data services; most of the extracted text is garbled OCR.
The Arabic title page of the second edition of the classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health.
The copyright and cataloguing page of the Arabic edition, with ISBNs, a note on the first edition's title and standard disclaimers; much of the Latin-script text is garbled OCR.
The Arabic table of contents, listing the acknowledgements, executive summary, health system challenges, intervention categories and annexes; the dot leaders are garbled.

Acknowledges those who coordinated the update and members of the WHO technical advisory group on classifications, including staff of regional offices. It also thanks partner agencies whose support made developing and updating the classification possible.

The executive summary defines digital health as the systematic use of information and communication technology and data to support decisions and improve health. It notes rapid innovation and explains that the former system categories have been renamed and reorganized as types of services and applications.

Lists the main changes in this edition, such as referring to people rather than clients, more inclusive language, added metadata and synonyms, and new interventions including pandemic-era capabilities. It ends by naming the renamed services and applications section and the main intervention groups.

Describes the classification as a shared language for how digital technologies serve health system needs, aimed at governments, technologists, providers, donors, implementers and researchers. It lists uses such as national strategies, legislation, training, research and capacity building.

Explains that the classification is organized around health system challenges in nine categories, digital interventions grouped by primary user, and types of services and applications. It gives an example linking targeted communication to under-use of services.

Explains how digital interventions map to types of services and applications, such as logistics information systems and electronic medical records, as a basis for interoperability. It includes a figure linking challenges, interventions and applications; parts of the text are garbled.

Presents use cases, the first showing how an immunization programme could analyse why new mothers miss vaccinations and choose a digital intervention to address it. Another use case describes searching a registry of digital health projects filtered by health focus.

Defines key terms: digital health intervention, digital health application and health system challenge, with examples such as loss to follow-up. A short reference list follows, with partly garbled URLs.
A near-blank page with only garbled characters.
A section divider for the part on digital interventions, services and applications.
Introduces the health system challenges framework as an overview of general problems that digital interventions can address and a starting point for programme planners.

Lists health system challenges by category, including information, availability, quality, acceptability, utilization, efficiency, cost, accountability and equity, with specific items under each. Some numbering in the extracted text is garbled.
Introduces the category of digital health interventions for persons, meaning members of the public and their caregivers who use health services.

An overview diagram of digital interventions for persons, such as targeted and untargeted communication, personal health tracking, citizen-based reporting and person-centred financial transactions. The extracted text is jumbled because of the diagram layout.

Describes targeted communication to persons, which sends health information to specific groups or individuals and may be tailored or two-way. It lists sub-interventions such as health event alerts and diagnostic results, with examples like sending test results to people who may not return to clinic.

Describes untargeted communication such as mass message campaigns, peer-group communication and personal health tracking. Examples include patient-managed personal health records and wearable fitness trackers.

Covers interventions for persons on actively capturing their own health data and accessing verifiable documents such as vaccination records. It also describes citizen-based reporting and on-demand health information, including booking appointments.

Describes simulated human-like conversations, such as AI chatbots, and person-centred financial transactions like mobile payments, vouchers and incentives. It also covers digital management of individuals' consent to the use and sharing of their health information.
Introduces the category of digital health interventions for health-care providers, who are health workers delivering interventions.

An overview diagram of digital interventions for health-care providers, such as identification and registration, health records, decision support, telemedicine, referral coordination, training and financial transactions. The extracted text is jumbled because of the diagram layout.

Describes provider interventions for identifying and registering people, including biometric verification, with examples such as fingerprint-based identification for TB treatment adherence. It also covers person-centred health records, citing open-source electronic medical record platforms.

Covers managing unstructured clinical records, collecting routine indicator data and provider decision support. Examples include checklists and mobile decision-support apps for screening pregnancy complications.

Describes telemedicine, including remote consultations between people and providers, telephone hotlines and remote monitoring with body sensor networks. It also introduces health worker communication, such as two-way SMS systems linking ministries and health workers.

Lists further provider communication interventions, such as feedback on performance, workflow notices, non-routine alerts and generative AI for tailored content. It also covers referral coordination, with examples of notifying facilities of incoming patients and tablet-based clinical algorithms.

Describes managing referrals between the health sector and other services such as social services, police and justice, citing examples like gender-based violence and malnutrition. It also covers health worker training and competency assessment, with a smartphone app that prompts workers with quiz questions.

A page of WHO's classification of digital health interventions (in Arabic) covering interventions for health care providers on managing prescriptions and medicines and on laboratory and diagnostic imaging, such as tracking prescription orders, reporting adverse drug effects and tracking biological specimens. Each category lists related terms and an illustrative example, though parts of the extracted text are garbled.

Describes the digital intervention category for providers' financial transactions, covering checking a person's eligibility for coverage and receiving payments for services, with illustrative examples.
Introduces the category of digital health interventions for health management and support staff, who manage and oversee health systems.

An overview chart of the digital interventions for health system managers, such as workforce management, supply chain, civil registration, health financing, equipment and facility management; the extracted Arabic text is heavily garbled.

Describes digital interventions for human resource management, including listing the health workforce, monitoring provider performance, managing certification and assigning activities to health workers, with examples. Parts of the extracted text are garbled.

Describes digital interventions for supply chain management, including stock management and distribution, reporting stock levels, registering licensed drugs, procurement and reporting counterfeit medicines. Examples include logistics information systems and an SMS-based drug authentication service.

Covers digital interventions for notifying public health events and for civil registration and vital statistics, such as event-based surveillance and notification and certification of births and deaths. It also begins the health financing category, including enrolment in and verification of health coverage schemes.

Continues the health financing interventions, such as insurance claims management, payments to facilities, payroll and incentives for health workers, budget planning and collecting insurance contributions. Examples include a Kenyan mobile platform for paying health insurance premiums.

Describes digital interventions for equipment and asset management and for facility management, such as tracking equipment maintenance, health facility registries and facility assessment and supervision. Some extracted text is garbled.
Describes digital interventions for managing person-centred health certificates, including registering, verifying, updating and revoking them, with digital immunization certificates as an example.
Introduces the category of digital health interventions for data services, which support data management, use and governance.

An overview chart of digital interventions for data services, covering data management, coding, location mapping, data exchange and interoperability and data governance; the extracted Arabic text is partly garbled.

Describes digital interventions for data management, including data collection, storage and aggregation, synthesis and visualization, and automated analysis for prediction, with examples such as dashboards and a labour monitoring prediction tool.

Describes digital interventions for data coding, such as parsing unstructured data, terminology standards and classifying disease or death codes, and for location mapping of facilities, events and households. Examples include an electronic diagnosis terminology tool and GPS-based mapping of spraying activities.
Covers mapping health worker locations, linking health data to geographic data, and data exchange and interoperability, such as a national health information exchange platform and message routing.
Describes digital interventions for data governance compliance, including identity authentication, consent management, protecting sensitive data and trust architecture, with illustrative examples.

Introduces the types of digital services and applications used to deliver digital health interventions and gives an overview table of the five groups, such as point-of-service systems, registries and directories, and data management services.
Describes point-of-service systems, starting with communication systems, clinical decision support and diagnostic information systems, listing their functional areas.
Describes further point-of-service systems, including electronic medical records, laboratory information systems, pharmacy information systems and telemedicine, with their functional areas.
Describes health system and provider administration systems, including blood bank information systems, health finance systems, programme monitoring systems and human resource information systems.
Describes learning and training systems, logistics management information systems, patient administration systems and research information systems, listing their functions.

Describes registries and directories, including census and population information systems, civil registration systems, community-based information systems, facility registries and health worker registries.
Describes identification registries, immunization information systems and terminology and classification systems based on international standards such as ICD.
Describes data management services, including analytics systems, data interchange and interoperability, data warehouses and environmental monitoring systems.
Describes geographic information systems, health management information systems, knowledge management systems and shared health records.
Describes surveillance and response systems, including emergency preparedness and response systems and public health and disease surveillance systems.
The start of the reference list for the definitions and examples of digital health interventions; the extracted text is largely garbled, with Latin-script citations rendered as Arabic characters.
Continuation of the reference list for the digital health intervention examples; the extracted text is almost entirely garbled OCR.
Continuation of the reference list for the digital health intervention examples; the extracted text is largely garbled, with only fragments of Arabic citations readable.
The reference list for the types of digital services and applications, citing WHO documents such as the digital implementation investment guide; parts of the extracted text are garbled.
A blank page with no extracted text.

Explains how WHO's classification of digital health interventions was developed, from the 2018 first edition based on mHealth categories and consultations to the revisions in the current edition, and gives links to examples and a feedback form.
A blank page with no extracted text.
A near-blank back cover page showing only fragments of an ISBN barcode number.
